prompt.context: Our client is a company that owns and operates retirement homes in the US. They just opened a new retirement home in Chicago about a year ago and they have concerns about its profitability. We were hired to fix the problem.
prompt.question: Why might the new retirement home be unprofitable, and what would you recommend to address the problem?

clarifying_info.q: Where is the new home located relative to existing homes?
clarifying_info.a: The new home is located in downtown Chicago. All previous homes were located outside of Miami.

clarifying_info.q: How many units does the new home have, and what is the revenue per unit?
clarifying_info.a: The new home has 400 units at $1,000/unit revenue. The typical (old) home has 800 units at $500/unit.

clarifying_info.q: What is the vacancy rate for the new vs. old homes?
clarifying_info.a: The new home has 10% vacancy. The old (typical) home has 20% vacancy.

clarifying_info.q: What are the main cost categories for operating the homes?
clarifying_info.a: Costs include: Amenities (fixed + variable per apartment), Maintenance, Utilities (variable per occupied apartment), Medical Facility, and SG&A.

clarifying_info.q: What are the amenities costs for each home?
clarifying_info.a: Old home: $48,000 total ($24,000 fixed + $30/month per apartment variable = $24,000 variable). New home: $54,000 total ($30,000 fixed + $60/month per apartment variable = $24,000 variable).

clarifying_info.q: What are the maintenance costs for each home?
clarifying_info.a: Old home: $100,000 total ($125/month per apartment variable). New home: $80,000 total ($200/month per apartment variable).

clarifying_info.q: What are the utilities costs for each home?
clarifying_info.a: Old home: $38,400 total ($60/month per occupied apartment; 640 occupied apartments). New home: $45,000 total ($125/month per occupied apartment; 360 occupied apartments).

clarifying_info.q: Does the new home have a medical facility?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. The new home has a medical facility costing $60,000. The old home does not.

clarifying_info.q: What are SG&A costs for each home?
Does the client own the land?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. The client owns the land for all retirement homes.

framework: Profitability = Revenue - Costs; diagnose whether the issue lies on the revenue or cost side
Revenue analysis: units, price per unit, vacancy rate, actual revenue
Cost analysis: break down by category (amenities, maintenance, utilities, medical facility, SG&A) — fixed vs. variable
Calculate margin in absolute and percentage terms for new vs. old homes
Compare new home performance to baseline (typical old home) to identify structural differences
Assess whether a true profitability problem exists; if not, identify cost optimization opportunities

questions.prompt: Calculate the actual revenue for the old (typical) home and the new Chicago home.
questions.guidance: Candidate should multiply units by revenue/unit to get total available revenue, then apply the vacancy rate to find actual revenue. Old home: 800 × $500 = $400,000 available; 20% vacancy means 80% occupied → $320,000 actual. New home: 400 × $1,000 = $400,000 available; 10% vacancy means 90% occupied → $360,000 actual.

math.answer: Old home actual revenue: $320,000. New home actual revenue: $360,000.

questions.prompt: Calculate total costs for the old and new homes across all cost categories and determine the margin for each.
questions.guidance: Candidate should sum all cost line items from each category and subtract from actual revenue to get margin, then compute gross margin %. Old: $266,400 costs → $53,600 margin (16.8%). New: $299,000 costs → $61,000 margin (16.9%). The new home has higher absolute costs but also higher revenues, yielding nearly identical margin percentages.

math.setup: Total Costs = Amenities + Maintenance + Utilities + Medical Facility + SG&A; Margin = Actual Revenue - Total Costs; Gross Margin % = Margin / Actual Revenue
math.answer: Old home: $53,600 margin (16.8%). New home: $61,000 margin (16.9%).

questions.prompt: What does the cost comparison reveal? Are there meaningful differences in cost structure between the two homes?
questions.guidance: Candidate should notice: (1) New home has a medical facility ($60,000) that old homes lack — likely due to downtown Chicago location or higher-end positioning. (2) New home has higher variable amenities ($60 vs $30/apartment). (3) New home has higher variable utilities ($125 vs $60/occupied apartment). (4) New home has lower maintenance total despite higher per-unit rate (fewer units). (5) New home has lower SG&A ($60K vs $80K). Despite higher costs, higher revenue offsets them.

brainstorming.prompt: Even though there is no profitability problem right now, what are opportunities to further reduce costs or improve margins across both the old and new homes?

categories.name: Amenities
ideas: Negotiate bulk contracts for amenity supplies across all locations
Audit whether fixed amenity costs ($30,000 in new home vs $24,000 in old) reflect necessary upgrades or waste
Standardize amenity packages to reduce per-unit variable cost in new home ($60 vs $30)

categories.name: Maintenance
ideas: Investigate why old home maintenance is $100,000 vs $80,000 despite lower per-unit rate — possibly older infrastructure
Implement preventive maintenance schedules to reduce long-run repair costs
Share maintenance staff or contracts across locations if geographically feasible

categories.name: Utilities
ideas: Invest in energy-efficient equipment to reduce $125/occupied unit in new home
Monitor occupancy patterns to optimize heating/cooling costs

categories.name: Medical Facility
ideas: Assess whether $60,000 medical facility cost is fixed or scalable with occupancy
Explore partnerships with local Chicago hospitals to share or offset medical facility costs
Evaluate whether adding medical facilities to old homes could justify higher revenue per unit

categories.name: SG&A
ideas: Leverage shared services or centralized back office across all retirement homes
Benchmark SG&A as % of revenue — new home at $60K/$360K ≈ 16.7%, old at $80K/$320K = 25%
Explore technology investments to reduce administrative overhead

categories.name: Revenue optimization
ideas: Reduce vacancy further below 10% in new home via targeted marketing in Chicago
Evaluate whether price per unit in old homes can be increased given low vacancy
Explore ancillary revenue streams (premium services, medical services for non-residents)

recommendation: The new Chicago retirement home does not have a profitability problem. Its margin ($61,000 / 16.9%) is actually slightly higher than the typical old home ($53,600 / 16.8%) in both absolute and percentage terms.

The concern likely stems from observing higher absolute costs ($299,000 vs $266,400), but these are offset by higher revenues driven by a higher price per unit ($1,000 vs $500) and lower vacancy (10% vs 20%).

We recommend the client recognize the new home is performing well, but investigate the differences in cost structure — particularly the medical facility and higher per-unit utility costs — to identify whether similar efficiencies can be applied across all locations.
risks: The new home is only one year old; costs may increase as the facility ages (especially maintenance)
The medical facility adds a fixed cost layer not present in old homes — if occupancy drops, margins compress faster
Downtown Chicago may face higher labor costs, regulatory requirements, or competition not yet fully reflected in year-one data
Comparison to outside-Miami homes may not be fully apples-to-apples given geographic and demographic differences
next_steps: Benchmark medical facility costs against industry norms for urban retirement homes
Analyze whether the old Miami homes could benefit from a price increase or amenity upgrades given their lower revenue per unit
Monitor new home cost trajectory over the next 1-2 years as initial operating period stabilizes
Explore opportunities to consolidate procurement (amenities, utilities, maintenance contracts) across all locations
